Your systems stay. We connect them.

We work with the software you already run, connect it through supported APIs, webhooks, or exports, and make the results measurable.

What we integrate with

Examples of systems commonly found in e-commerce. Naming a product does not imply a partnership; integrations depend on the APIs and exports your plan provides.

  • Storefront and checkout

    Source of product views, carts, orders and customer accounts. Its webhooks and APIs trigger most journeys, and results are written back to the order.

    • Shopify
    • WooCommerce
    • Adobe Commerce (Magento)
    • Custom Next.js storefronts

  • Marketplaces and quick commerce

    Channels where listings, stock and prices must stay consistent. We connect through official seller APIs, or scheduled partner upload files where no API exists.

    • Amazon Seller Central
    • Flipkart Seller Hub
    • Myntra and Ajio
    • Nykaa
    • Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart

  • Order and warehouse management

    System of record for sellable stock, batches, serial numbers and order states, and the source for inventory sync and dispatch.

    • Unicommerce
    • EasyEcom
    • Increff
    • Vinculum

  • Shipping and courier aggregators

    Provides tracking events, NDR reasons and reverse pickups. We normalize their status codes and send reattempt instructions back.

    • Shiprocket
    • Delhivery
    • Blue Dart
    • Shadowfax
    • Xpressbees

  • Payments and finance

    Payment links, refunds and settlement data. Card data stays inside the gateway's PCI DSS environment and never enters our workflows.

    • Razorpay
    • Cashfree
    • PayU
    • Stripe for international stores
    • Tally or Zoho Books

  • Support, CRM and messaging

    Where conversations, tickets and consent live. Automations write back summaries, tags and outcomes so agents see one history.

    • Freshdesk
    • Zendesk
    • Gorgias
    • WhatsApp Business Solution Providers
    • Klaviyo

  • Distribution and retailer ordering

    Retailer, scheme and credit data for B2B reorders in FMCG. The sales rep or distributor confirms every order before dispatch.

    • Bizom
    • Distributor ERP
    • SAP Business One
    • Tally

The measures we propose to track

We agree the definition, population, period, source, and owner of each measure before launch.

Return-to-origin (RTO) rate
Share of shipped orders returned to origin without delivery, split by payment mode, pincode, courier and campaign.Why it matters: Each return to origin pays freight twice and locks stock. It is the clearest test of whether confirmation and NDR work is paying off.
COD confirmation rate
Share of COD orders confirmed by the shopper before dispatch, out of all COD orders created in the period.Why it matters: Shows whether confirmation messages reach shoppers and which orders should be held rather than shipped.
NDR resolution before cut-off
Share of failed delivery attempts where a shopper response and courier instruction were recorded before the courier's reattempt cut-off.Why it matters: A failed attempt is the last chance to save a parcel; speed and verification decide whether it is delivered or returned.
Listing completeness
Share of live SKUs with every mandatory declaration and required channel attribute present and approved.Why it matters: Incomplete listings get suppressed, mislead shoppers and create Legal Metrology and consumer-protection risk.
Stock-out cancellations
Orders canceled after acceptance because stock was not available, per channel and SKU.Why it matters: Overselling damages marketplace ratings and shopper trust, and shows whether sync and buffers are working.
First response time
Median time from a shopper's message to the first meaningful reply, by channel and topic, within agreed service hours.Why it matters: Fast, correct first replies prevent cancellations and repeat contacts, especially on sale days.
AI handoff rate and groundedness
Share of assistant conversations handed to an agent, and share of sampled answers fully supported by approved sources.Why it matters: Shows whether the assistant helps without improvising policy, and where the knowledge base needs work.
Return-to-exchange share
Share of eligible return requests the shopper chose to convert into an exchange or store credit.Why it matters: Exchanges keep revenue and reveal size and fit issues. The measure must reflect shopper choice, not pressure.
Repeat purchase rate
Share of first-time buyers in a monthly cohort who place a second order within the agreed window for the category.Why it matters: Repeat orders carry D2C economics; it is the outcome retention and replenishment journeys should move.
Marketing opt-out rate
Share of delivered marketing messages followed by an opt-out or block, per channel and journey.Why it matters: Protects consent, sender reputation and WhatsApp quality ratings, and flags journeys that annoy rather than help.

How we connect systems responsibly

  • Client-owned accounts, data and credentials; we work through agreed roles and permissions.
  • Integrations use official APIs, webhooks or exports where the system provides them; nothing scrapes private portals.
  • Every automation has a named owner, an exception queue and a manual fallback.
  • Messages, prompts and templates are reviewed and approved by the client before launch.
  • AI outputs are grounded in approved sources and checked against an agreed evaluation set before release.
